﴿Say: It has been revealed to me that a company of the jinn listened, and they said: "Indeed, we have heard an amazing Qur'an. It guides to right conduct, so we have believed in it, and we will never associate anyone with our Lord."﴾

Page 218

The opening of the surah with the command to speak indicates that what follows is a strange event, especially for the polytheists, who are the most likely to deny it, as His saying indicates: ﴿as you assumed that Allah would never resurrect anyone﴾ [al-Jinn: 7], as will come.

Allah commanded His Messenger ﷺ to inform the Muslims and others that Allah had revealed to him the occurrence of a great event in his call. Allah established it as an honour for His Prophet and as a distinction for the Qur'an: He subjected some of the species called jinn to listen to the Qur'an, inspired them, or taught them, to understand what they heard, and guided them to the extent of his guidance to the truth, to monotheism, to the glorification of Allah, and to belief in resurrection and recompense. Thus the call of Islam, in its foundations, reached a world of the unseen worlds, to whose beings the obligations and the creeds have no relation. Rather, it is a world whose people are disposed to what they were created with, of good or evil, and none of them transgresses his disposition during the period of the world, so that his eternal destiny in the Hereafter is according to its measure. For this reason, He did not send to them legislations.

Allah has revealed to this group among them realities of the creed and guidance of Islam, and they understood it.

This world is the world of the jinn. According to what is deduced from the apparent meanings of the Qur'an and from the sound and fair prophetic reports, it is a kind of the immaterial (al-mujarradat), that is, the subtle beings that are not dense, hidden from the sense of sight and hearing, spread in unknown places, not on the surface of the earth nor in the heavens, but in unbounded atmospheres. They belong to the category of substance among the immaterial substances, that is: they are not bodies nor corporeal things, but spiritual beings created from a fiery element, having life, will, and a perception specific to them whose extent is not known. These fiery immaterial beings are a genus among the genera of substances, comprising the jinn and the devils; they are two species of the genus of fiery immaterial beings, having particular perceptions and limited dispositions. They are hidden from view, attached to the world of the unseen, not seen by eyes, nor perceived by the ears of people, except when Allah conveys the awareness of their movements and wills to humans in the manner of a miracle, a breaking of custom, for a matter Allah has decreed and willed.

By the mutual support of these proofs and their reinforcement of one another, although each one of them is merely speculative in its indication, namely the apparent meanings of the Qur'an, or speculative in its text and indication, namely the sound hadiths, there results what necessitates the belief in the existence of hidden beings called the jinn, and by this the meanings of verses of the Qur'an and reports of the Sunnah are explained.

Even if there are among them some who are not accused of lying, yet it is what is cited as an example in the saying of al-Ma'arri:

"Like you, one who imagined and then became a friend..."

The mention of the jinn has already passed at His saying ﴿and they made the jinn partners with Allah﴾ [al-An'am: 100] in Surat al-An'am, and at His saying ﴿And We have certainly created for Hell many of the jinn and mankind﴾ [al-A'raf: 179] in Surat al-A'raf.

Those to whom the Messenger ﷺ was commanded to say that it had been revealed to him concerning the account of the jinn are all the people to whom the Prophet ﷺ conveyed the Qur'an, from among the Muslims and the polytheists. Allah willed that this report be conveyed to them because of what it indicates of the nobility of this religion, the nobility of its Book, and the nobility of the one who brought it. It contains a joy for the Muslims and an implicit rebuke for the polytheists, since the jinn had perceived the nobility of the Qur'an and understood its purposes, though they do not know its language nor perceive its eloquence, so they turned to it; while those to whose language it was revealed and who perceived the distinctive features of its eloquence denied it and turned away from it.

In the statement that the report of the jinn's listening to the Qur'an was revealed to him, there is an indication that he did not know of that except by Allah's informing him of the occurrence of this listening. Thus the verse implies that the Messenger ﷺ did not know of the presence of the jinn for listening to the Qur'an before the revelation of this verse.

As for the verse of al-Ahqaf ﴿And when We turned to you a company of the jinn listening to the Qur'an﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 29] and what follows, it is either a reminder of what is in this verse, or an allusion to another story narrated by 'Abdullah ibn Mas'ud, which is in Sahih Muslim in the hadiths on recitation in prayers, and it has no connection with this verse.

His saying ﴿that a company of the jinn listened﴾ is in the position of the deputy subject of (أُوحِيَ, "it was revealed"), that is: there was revealed to me the listening of a company. The emphasis of the revealed report with the particle (أنَّ, "that") is for the sake of giving it importance because of its strangeness.

The pronoun in (أنَّهُ, "that it") is the pronoun of the matter, and its predicate is the clause ﴿a company of the jinn listened﴾; in this there is an increase of emphasis on the revealed report.

The object of (اسْتَمَعَ, "listened") is omitted, indicated by ﴿Indeed, we have heard a Qur'an﴾, that is: a company of the jinn listened to the Qur'an.

The nafar (نَفَرٌ) is a group from one to ten. Its original meaning in the language is a group of humans, and it was applied to a group of jinn by way of likeness, since there is no other word in the language, just as rijal (رِجالٌ, "men") was applied to the jinn in His saying ﴿some men from among the jinn used to seek refuge with men﴾ [al-Jinn: 6], to refer to the persons of the jinn. Their saying ﴿Indeed, we have heard an amazing Qur'an﴾ was said to some of them who had not been present for the listening to the Qur'an, whom Allah inspired to warn them and guide them to righteousness, as He said in Surat al-Ahqaf: ﴿And when We turned to you a company of the jinn listening to the Qur'an; and when they attended it, they said, "Be silent." And when it was concluded, they went back to their people as warners. They said, "O our people, indeed we have heard a Book..."﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 29] and so on.

The meaning of "saying" here is conveying their intention to those whom they wish to convey it to, from their own kind, in the manner by which they understand one another, since, as far as appears, the jinn have no words that flow on tongues. Thus "saying" here is used metaphorically for expressing what is in the soul, like His saying ﴿An ant said, "O ants, enter your dwellings"﴾ [al-Naml: 18]. In that case it is an honouring of this religion, that Allah made for it callers from the two weighty kinds (humans and jinn).

It may also be an inner saying, that is: thoughts that circulated in their perceptions with the circulation of speech that springs from the will of the one who perceives, to convey his perceptions to others. Such a thing is expressed by "saying," as in the verse of al-Nabighah describing a hunting dog:

"The self said to it: 'I see no hope,
and indeed your master has neither escaped nor hunted.'"

Among this is His saying ﴿And they say to themselves, "Why does Allah not punish us for what we say?"﴾ [al-Mujadilah: 8].

The emphasis of the report with (أنَّ) is because they reported it to a group among them who doubted its occurrence, so they used in their speech what confirms the truth of what they said, and this is what in Arabic is expressed by the particle (إنَّ) for such a case.

The description of the Qur'an as "amazing" ('ajab) is a description by the verbal noun for intensity of meaning, that is: one is amazed by it, and the meaning of that is that it is wondrous and unsurpassed in its content.

They gained knowledge of the Qur'an's excellences through an unveiling that Allah granted them. Al-Mazari said in his commentary on Sahih Muslim: "Whoever believes upon hearing the Qur'an must know the reality of its inimitability and the conditions of a miracle. After that, knowledge of the truthfulness of the Messenger occurs; either the jinn knew that, or they knew from the books of earlier messengers what indicated to them that he is the unlettered Prophet, truthful, whose coming was foretold." End of quote. I say: the jinn gained new knowledge of that through inspiration from Allah, by proofs they were not aware of, since they were not obliged to know them; and their understanding of the Qur'an was of the kind of inspiration that Allah created in them in a manner that breaks custom, as an honour to the Messenger ﷺ and to the Qur'an.

Belief in the Qur'an necessitates belief in the one who brought it and in the one who sent it down, and for this reason they said ﴿and we will never associate anyone with our Lord﴾.

These company of jinn attained the honour of knowing Allah and His attributes, the truthfulness of His Messenger ﷺ, the truthfulness of the Qur'an, and what it contains, from what they heard of it; so they became among the choicest of creatures, and were honoured with success in the Hereafter, and were not among those whom Allah created for Hell from the jinn and mankind.

The object of (اسْتَمَعَ, "listened") is omitted, indicated by His saying after it: ﴿So they said, "Indeed, we have heard an amazing Qur'an."﴾

Al-Rushd (الرُّشْدِ): with a dammah on the ra' and a sukun on the shin (rushd), or it may be said with a fathah on the ra' and a fathah on the shin (rashad); it means goodness, correctness, and guidance. The ten recitations agree on reciting it with a dammah then a sukun.

Their saying ﴿and we will never associate anyone with our Lord﴾ means that this negation holds in the future. This implies that they had been polytheists, and for this reason they emphasised the negation of association with the particle of permanence (لَنْ). Just as their report about the Qur'an and praise of it was emphasised with (إنَّ), their report about their abandonment of association was emphasised with (لَنْ).

Page 222
﴿And He, exalted is the majesty of our Lord; He has not taken a consort nor a son.﴾
This is related from the speech of the jinn. The majority (al-Jumhur) read the hamza of (innahu) with a kasra, considering it coordinated with their saying ﴿Indeed, we have heard a wondrous Qur'an﴾ [al-Jinn: 1], since the hamza of (inna) must be kasra when it is reported after a saying.

Ibn 'Amir, Hamza, al-Kisa'i, Hafs, Abu Ja'far and Khalaf read it with a fatha on the hamza, considering it coordinated with the pronoun in the preposition bi- in His saying ﴿so we believed in Him﴾ [al-Jinn: 2], i.e., "and we believed that exalted is the majesty of our Lord." Not repeating the preposition with a conjunct of a noun governed by a particle is in use, and the Kufans permitted it, since the omission of the preposition with (anna) is common, so there should be no disagreement about omitting it here by interpretation.

Al-Zamakhshari said in al-Kashshaf: (﴿That He, the jinn listened﴾ [al-Jinn: 1]) with fatha, because it is the agent of (uhiya), i.e., the deputy of the agent; (﴿And that we heard﴾ [al-Jinn: 1]) with kasra, because it is a subject reported after a saying. Then the rest are construed upon these two: whatever is from the revelation has fatha, and whatever is from the speech of the jinn has kasra. All of them are from the speech of the jinn except the other two: ﴿And that the mosques are for Allah﴾ [al-Jinn: 18] and ﴿And that when the servant of Allah stood﴾ [al-Jinn: 19]. As for whoever reads all of them with fatha, it is by coordination with the locative position of the preposition and its object in ﴿we believed in Him﴾ [al-Jinn: 13], as if it were said: "we affirmed Him and affirmed that exalted is the majesty of our Lord, and that our foolish one used to say," and likewise the rest. End of quotation.

Ta'ali means extreme elevation. It is treated as one who exerts himself to be elevated, because his elevation goes beyond what people commonly know, so it resembles affectation.

Al-Jadd, with fatha on the jim, means greatness and majesty. This is a preface and introduction to His saying ﴿He has not taken a consort nor a son﴾, because taking a consort is for need of her, for her companionship and help and the enjoyment of her company, and all of this is among the signs of need. Allah, exalted is He, is the absolutely Self-Sufficient, and exalted is His majesty in His absolute independence. A son is desired for help and companionship, along with what it entails of being a separated part of his parents; all of this is from need and deficiency.

The pronoun in (innahu) is a pronoun of the matter (damir al-sha'n), and its predicate is the clause ﴿exalted is the majesty of our Lord﴾.

The clause ﴿He has not taken a consort﴾ to its end is a substitute of inclusion (badal ishtimal) from the clause ﴿exalted is the majesty of our Lord﴾.

And the foolish among us used to speak about God an outrageous lie. Most readers recited the hamza of ﴿وإنَّهُ﴾ with a kasra (*wa-innahu*). Ibn 'Amir, Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, Hafs, Abu Ja'far and Khalaf recited it with a fatha (*wa-annahu*), as was explained earlier in His words ﴿وأنَّهُ تَعالى جَدُّ رَبِّنا﴾ [al-Jinn: 3]. Their belief in the exaltedness of God above taking a consort or a son may have arisen from what they heard of the Qur'an, or it may have arisen from their own grasp of this through speculative proofs.

Al-safih (the foolish one) here is a collective noun. It was said that they meant Iblis, that is, that he used to instruct them in attributes of God unbefitting His majesty. That is, they used to speak an outrageous lie about God before the Qur'an was revealed, by their foolishness in this matter.

Al-shatat (the outrageous) is exceeding the limit and that which departs from justice and correctness. It was mentioned earlier in His words ﴿ولا تُشْطِطْ﴾ [Sad: 22] in Surat Sad, meaning "and do not deviate." What is meant by al-shatat is the affirmation of what His words ﴿ولَنْ نُشْرِكَ بِرَبِّنا أحَدًا﴾ [al-Jinn: 2] and His words ﴿ما اتَّخَذَ صاحِبَةً ولا ولَدًا﴾ [al-Jinn: 3] deny, meaning "and we shall never associate anyone with our Lord" and "He has taken neither a consort nor a son." The pronoun in ﴿وإنَّهُ﴾ is the pronoun of the matter (*damir al-sha'n*), which refers forward to the subject of the statement.

The discussion of this, and of the emphatic particle *inna* whether kasra or fatha, is the same as the discussion of His words ﴿وإنَّهُ تَعالى جَدُّ رَبِّنا﴾ [al-Jinn: 3], and so on.

﴿And indeed we thought that no human or jinn would ever speak a lie against Allah.﴾

The hamza of (inna) is read with a kasra by the majority of readers (al-Jumhur) and Abu Ja'far, while Ibn 'Amir, Hafs, Hamzah, al-Kisa'i and Khalaf read it with a fatha.

The majority of reciters read the hamza of (wa-innahu) with a kasra. Al-ʿawdh (seeking refuge) is taking shelter in that which saves one from a harmful thing. So the frightened person would shout at the top of his voice: "O Master (ʿaziz) of this valley, I seek refuge in You from the foolish ones who are in Your obedience," and he would imagine that the jinni in the valley would protect him. They said: the first to establish this practice for them were a people from Yemen, then the Banu Hanifa, then this spread among the Arabs. These are delusions and imaginings.

The people of this interpretation claim that the meaning of ﴿so they increased them in distress﴾ is that the jinn used to look down upon mankind because of this fear, so they would frequently confront them and appear to them, thereby increasing their fear.

What I choose as the meaning of the verse is that al-ʿawdh here is seeking refuge in a thing and clinging to it. The intended meaning is that there were a people among the polytheists who worshipped the jinn in order to guard against their evil. The meaning of ﴿so they increased them in distress﴾ is: their worship of them increased them in misguidance. Al-rahaq is applied to sin (al-ithm).

*So I said: By God's oath, I will not leave staying*

The *lam* in His saying (*li-al-sam'*) is the *lam* of cause, meaning: for the sake of hearing, that is, so that we might hear what happens in the upper world of the angels' disposing and arranging. The *min* is partitive, that is, from its courtyards, and it is connected to (*naq'udu*, we sit). The governed phrase is not a circumstantial clause (*hal*) of (*maqa'id*) placed before its referent, because the context is about their state in the heaven, so the concern with what is connected to the verb of sitting takes priority. *The tick walks upon it, then slides from it, and the flank's fat (labban) and the closest of the hard tufts (zahalil).*

So his saying (*minha*) is connected to the verb (*yuzliquhu*, slides), not a circumstantial clause of (*laban*).

The use of this word (*maqa'id*) in this position is correct, but it agrees with what is disliked to mention, especially since it is attributed to something that may be attributed to it, that is, what is disliked, namely the visitors (*al-'uwwad*). The *fa'* (so) which introduces (﴿So whoever listens now will find for himself a watching meteor﴾) is a consequence of an omitted element indicated by the verb (*kunna*, we used to). The word (*al-an*, now) corresponds to (*kunna*, we used to); that is, that was then and it has ended.

The conditional form and its response were used in the consequence to warn their brethren against approaching listening, because the listener exposes himself to the harm of meteors.

The jinn do not refrain from that, because they are driven to it by nature, along with the harm they suffer from stoning and burning. This is like the drive of creatures toward what they were created for, such as moths hurling themselves into fire. This is because the thinking faculty in the jinn may be weak, so that desire dominates it. We see humans plunging into dangers and perils following their passions, such as the ventures of amateurs in seas, mountains and snows.

The occurrence of *shihaban* (a meteor) in a conditional context indicates generality, because the conditional context has the status of a negative context in conveying the generality of an indefinite noun.

*Al-rasad* is a collective noun for *rasid*, which is one who guards something. It is an adjective of (*shihaban*), meaning: watching meteors. Describing them with *rasad* is a metaphor, likened to watching guards. This is an allusion to the end of soothsaying, since the soothsayer receives from a jinni vague reports, with what the jinni snatches of the news of the unseen, snatching it incompletely. The soothsayer completes it by his conjecture, in accordance with the course of the circumstances of his people and his land. In a hadith: "Then he adds to that one word a hundred lies."

This is a consequence of their saying (﴿And indeed, we used to sit in it in positions for listening﴾ [al-Jinn: 9]) and so on; for that listening was for knowing what command was issued by God to the angels and what He informs them of, which He wishes to make them aware of. Thus they had knowledge of some of what they would snatch up. When they were prevented from listening, they no longer knew anything of that, so they informed their brethren of this, perhaps they would take heed from the causes of this change, and believe in the Revelation which God guarded from anyone's becoming aware of it before the one to whom it is revealed and the one who carries it to him.

The essential meaning is: "We now do not know what evil or good is intended for the people of the earth, after we used to spy on news in the heaven."

This is a preparation for what they will say: (﴿And indeed, among us are the righteous﴾ [al-Jinn: 11]), then their saying (﴿And indeed, we thought that we would never escape God on the earth﴾ [al-Jinn: 12]), then their saying (﴿And indeed, when we heard the guidance, we believed in it﴾ [al-Jinn: 13]), up to His words ﴿So they became fuel for Hell﴾ [al-Jinn: 15].

The object of (nadri, "we know") is what is indicated by the interrogative following it, in His words ﴿Is evil intended for those upon the earth, or does their Lord intend for them guidance?﴾, and it is this which suspends the verb (nadri) from operating. The interrogative is genuine, and the custom of grammarians regarding such a case is to posit an object drawn from the interrogative, its estimate being: "we do not know the answer to this question," and that is an estimate of meaning, not an estimate of grammatical analysis. This is the explanation of the verse according to the most complete meaning, and it is of the same kind as His saying, exalted is He, ﴿And I do not know what will be done with me or with you﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 9].

In our view, the intent of it is not that they deny knowing what God intended by these meteors, for that is not consistent with what preceded, that they believed in the Qur'an when they said (﴿Indeed, we have heard a wondrous Qur'an, guiding to right conduct, so we believed in it﴾ [al-Jinn: 1]) and their saying ﴿Whoever listens now will find for himself a watching flame﴾ [al-Jinn: 9]. That is explicit that they know that God intended good for those upon the earth through this religion and through turning the jinn away from eavesdropping.

The repetition of (inna) and its subject is for emphasis, because this report is exposed to the doubt of the listening jinn who had not tested the guarding of the heaven.

Al-rashad (guidance): attaining the intended beneficial goal, and it is a means to good; for this reason it is made the opposite of evil, and the verb of intending evil is attributed to the passive, and it is not attributed to God, exalted is He, even though its opposite is attributed to Him in His words ﴿or does their Lord intend for them guidance?﴾, in following the obligatory courtesy toward God, exalted is He, in avoiding attributing evil to Him.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 72, verse 11:

﴿And among us are the righteous, and among us are those beneath that; we have been of divergent paths.﴾

Page 232
The majority of reciters, and Abu Ja'far, read the hamza with a kasra (wa-annā). Ibn 'Amir, Hamza, al-Kisa'i, Hafs and Khalaf read it with a fatha (wa-annā), and it is part of the speech of the jinn.

The reading with a fatha on the hamza is a conjunction with the object of the preposition bi- (in "āmannā bi-"), meaning: "We believed that we are among the righteous," i.e., we became certain of this, while we had been in ignorance of it.

The signs of divine guidance became apparent upon them, so they knew that they had become two groups: a group of the righteous and a group that is not righteous. By "the righteous" they mean themselves, and by "those beneath that" the remainder of their kind who are below the level of righteousness. When they took the position of calling their brethren to follow the path of goodness, they did not openly charge them with corruption; rather, they were inspired and said, "Among us are the righteous." Then they were gentle and said, "and among us are those beneath that," which covers those who stand at various degrees of evil and corruption, so that the addressees would seek the indications that distinguish the two groups. Moreover, they left room for the possibility that "the righteous" might refer to those who are perfect in righteousness, so that "those beneath that" would refer to those who fall short of the rank of perfection in righteousness. This is among the eloquent expressions in calling to and guiding toward goodness.

Dūn: a noun meaning "beneath" (taḥt), the opposite of fawq (above). For this reason its accusative is frequently used as a spatial adverb of place, i.e., in a place lower than the righteous.

The estimated meaning is: "And among us is a group in a rank beneath them."

The adverbial sense of dūn is figurative. The adverbial phrase here functions as a stable adverbial complement in the position of an adjective modifying an omitted noun, whose estimate is "a group" (farīq), as in His saying, exalted is He, ﴿وما مِنّا إلّا لَهُ مَقامٌ مَعْلُومٌ﴾ [al-Saffat: 164]. The omission of the modified noun is regular when it is part of a noun governed by the preposition min preceding it and the adjective is an adverbial phrase, as here, or a clause, as in the Arabs' saying: "Among us is one who departed and among us is one who stayed."

His saying, ﴿كُنّا طَرائِقَ قِدَدًا﴾, is an eloquent simile: it likens the divergence of conditions and beliefs to paths, each of which leads to a place that the others do not lead to.

Ṭarā'iq: the plural of ṭarīqa, and the ṭarīqa is the ṭarīq (path). Perhaps it is specific to the wide, clear path, since the tā' is for emphasis, like dār and dāra, and maqām and maqāma. For this reason the orbits of the stars were likened to it in His saying, ﴿ولَقَدْ خَلَقْنا فَوْقَكم سَبْعَ طَرائِقَ﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 17], and it was described as "the best" in His saying, ﴿ويَذْهَبا بِطَرِيقَتِكُمُ المُثْلى﴾ [Ta-Ha: 63].

The description of ṭarā'iq with qidadan, which is a collective noun of qidda (with a kasra on the qaf and a shadda on the dal), and the qidda is a strip of leather or the like cut lengthwise like a thong. The paths were likened, in their multiplicity, to the strips cut from hide, which the maker of leather thongs cuts, with which they used to bind captives.

The meaning: they call their brethren to unity of belief by following the guidance of Islam. The statement is thus used allusively to censure the disagreement among the people, and that it is incumbent upon them to unite and seek the truth, so that their unity may be upon the truth.

The purpose is not the informational content of the statement, since the addressees already know that; and the emphasis by inna is directed at the allusive meaning.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 72, verse 12:

﴿And indeed we thought that we would never escape Allah in the earth, nor escape Him by fleeing.﴾

The majority of readers, and Abu Ja'far, read the hamza of (wa-innā) with a kasra. Ibn 'Amir, Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, Hafs and Khalaf read it with a fatha, as a conjunction governing the genitive in the phrase ﴿fa-āmannā bihi﴾ [al-Jinn: 2]. The implied sense is: "and we believed that we would never escape Allah in the earth." The mention of the verb (ẓanannā) is a verbal emphasis of the verb (āmannā), understood through the conjunction particle, because faith is certainty, and ẓann (supposition) is used here to mean certainty, which is a common usage.

Since the state of righteousness is that it is pleasing to Allah the Exalted, and the state of its opposite is the reverse, as Allah the Exalted said ﴿And Allah does not love corruption﴾ [al-Baqarah: 205], they followed this with something that implies a warning to abandon the opposite of righteousness: that Allah has prepared a punishment for those who are not righteous. Thus they became certain that the punishment of Allah does not escape anyone who deserves it. They placed this before the command to believe found in His words (﴿And when we heard the guidance﴾ [al-Jinn: 13]) and what follows, because the warding off of harms takes precedence over the acquisition of benefits, and clearing away takes precedence over adorning. They gained knowledge of this from what they heard of the Qur'an, and they had not known it before, since they had not been addressed with instruction in the foundations of creed. When Allah inspired them to listen to the Qur'an, they learned the foundations of creed, and they warned their brethren against adopting polytheism and attributing to Allah what does not befit Him, because false belief is not upheld by sound perception once it has been made aware of its falsehood. Allah made this group of jinn a warner to their brethren and a guide to the truth to which the Qur'an had guided them. This does not imply that the jinn are under obligation to the legal rulings of Islam.

As for His words, the Exalted ﴿And We have certainly created for Hell many of the jinn and mankind; they have hearts with which they do not understand﴾ [al-A'raf: 179], and what follows, it indicates that their punishment is for disbelief and association of partners with Allah. Or it is meant that by "the jinn" are intended the devils, since the devils are of the kind of the jinn.

Al-i'jaz (making incapable) means making another incapable, i.e., unable to accomplish a matter, with a mention accompanied by what indicates incapacity. It is used here as a metaphor (kinayah) for escape and deliverance, like the saying of Iyas ibn Qabisah al-Ta'i:

Did you not see that the earth is vast and wide, so would any patch of its expanses incapacitate me?

That is: it does not escape me, nor does it go beyond my power.

The mention of "in the earth" indicates that the intended meaning of flight in His words ﴿nor escape Him by fleeing﴾ is flight from being pelted with shooting stars, i.e., "do not hope to eavesdrop, for the pelting of shooting stars in the sky will not miss you." They began the warning with the punishment of this world, to bring their people down gently.

It is also possible that the first (nu'jiza) means "to overcome," as in His words ﴿So they are not able to escape﴾ [al-Nahl: 46], i.e., they do not overcome Our power, and "in the earth" is intended to generalize the places, as in His words ﴿And you are not able to escape in the earth﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 22], i.e., in whatever place you may be. The meaning is: we do not overcome Allah by strength. The second (nu'jiza) means "escape," and for this reason it is clarified by "fleeing"; "fleeing" is a metaphor for slipping away from what Allah intended to inflict upon them of pelting and burning.

The word (ẓann) here is used to mean certainty, as indicated by the emphasis of the supposed matter by the particle (lan), which denotes the perpetuity and emphasis of negation.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 72, verse 13:

﴿And indeed, when we heard the guidance, we believed in it. So whoever believes in his Lord will not fear any loss or any humiliation.﴾

The majority of reciters, and Abu Ja'far, read (innā) with a kasra on the hamza. Ibn 'Amir, Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, Hafs and Khalaf read it with a fatha, as a conjunction (ʿaṭf) on the genitive in His saying ﴿فَآمَنَّا بِهِ﴾ [al-Jinn: 2].

The intended object of the conjunction is His saying ﴿whoever believes in his Lord will not fear any loss or any humiliation﴾, while the clause ﴿when we heard the guidance, we believed in it﴾ is a preparatory introduction to that.

Page 235
After they had warned their people of God's punishment in this world, or were reassured by recalling it to their own souls, they returned to encouraging them to believe in God alone and warning them against disbelief by way of implication (mafhum). By "the guidance" (al-huda) is meant the Qur'an, since it is what they heard, and they described it as guidance to emphasize that it is guiding.
The meaning of ﴿believes in his Lord﴾ is: believes in His existence and in His being singular in divinity, as is suggested by the mention of His name under the title "Lord" (al-Rabb), since the Lord is the Creator, and what does not create is not worshipped.

The clause ﴿whoever believes in his Lord will not fear any loss or any humiliation﴾ may be part of the speech reported from the jinn. It may also be words from God addressed to the polytheists, and it is then a parenthetical insertion (i'tiraḍ) between the two conjoined clauses.

Al-bakhs (loss) is being defrauded in a reward or the like.

Al-rahaq is disgrace, that is: he does not fear that he will be defrauded in the recompense for his faith, nor that he will be humiliated. From this is understood that whoever does not believe will be humiliated by punishment. The difference over the kasra and fatha of the hamza of (innā) is like the difference over the one preceding it.

The clause ﴿will not fear any loss or any humiliation﴾ is the answer to the condition of (man), which is made in the form of a nominal sentence, so it is joined with the fa' even though what follows the fa' is a verb. The rule for the answer of a condition is that it is not joined with the fa' unless it is unsuitable to be the verb of the condition. So its joining with the fa', when it is an imperfect verb, indicates an intention to make it the predicate of an omitted subject, so that the clause becomes nominal; and a nominal clause takes the fa' when it is the answer of a condition. Thus the estimated reading here is: "so he does not fear," so that it indicates the certainty of his safety from fear of loss and humiliation, and so that it indicates his being singled out for this, to the exclusion of others who do not believe in their Lord. The positing of the subject before the verbal predicate implies specification (takhsis) at one time and emphasis (taqwiya) at another, and both may coincide, as stated in His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿God mocks them﴾ [al-Baqarah: 15]. Both coincide here, as al-Zamakhshari indicated in the Kashshaf with his words: it indicates the certainty that the believer is saved without doubt, and that he is the one specially so, to the exclusion of others. The Kashshaf's statement is limited to explaining the excellence of the nominal clause, and it implies justifying the departure from the jussive form of the verb for this reason.

It may also be said: the departure from stripping the verb of the fa' and from jazm (jussive) is to averting the impression that (lā) is prohibitive (nāhiya). This departure is thus explicit in intending a promise, without the possibility of intending a prohibition.

In al-Damamini's commentary on al-Tashil, it is stated that when the answer of the condition is a verb negated with (lā), it is permissible to join it with the fa' or to omit it. I have not seen this in anyone else's work, and the Kashshaf's statement implies that joining with the fa' is obligatory unless another distinction is intended.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 72, verse 14:

﴿And indeed, among us are the Muslims, and among us are the deviators.﴾

The majority of readers (al-Jumhur) and Abu Ja'far recited the hamza with a kasra (wa-inna), while Ibn 'Amir, Hamza, al-Kisa'i, Hafs and Khalaf recited it with a fatha (wa-anna). The fatha reading is part of the speech of the jinn, and it is in coordination (ʿatf) with the object governed by the preposition bi (in the phrase "fa-amannā bihi," "so we believed in it"). The purpose of the coordination is His saying ﴿Whoever submits, those have sought out a right course﴾, and what precedes it is a preparatory statement (tawti'ah) for it. That is: after hearing the Qur'an, we have become: among us are the Muslims, meaning those who followed what Islam brought, in a manner suited to their condition; and among us are the qasitun, meaning the disbelievers who turn away. This is an elaboration of their statement (﴿And indeed, among us are the righteous, and among us are those below that﴾ [al-Jinn: 11]), because in it there is an explicit statement that what is "below that" is the opposite of righteousness.

It is apparent that the words extend to the end of what is related from the jinn of the perceptions expressed by "say" (al-qawl) and what is coordinated with it.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 72, verse 15:

﴿Whoever among them submits, those have sought out the right path.﴾ [al-Jinn: 14] ﴿As for those who deviate, they will be fuel for Hell.﴾ The apparent meaning is that this is outside the speech reported from the jinn, and that it is a statement from Allah, the Exalted, admonishing the polytheists among mankind; so it has the sense of a concluding remark (tadhyil). It is linked with the particle fa' (fa-) because it is a consequence of the narrative, drawing a lesson from it. So the consequence is the consequence of one statement upon another, not the consequence of the meaning of one statement upon the meaning of the statement before it.

Al-tahharri (seeking out, aiming for): seeking out al-hara, with two fathas, a defective word of the waw type, which is that which ought to be done. It is said: "bil-hariyy an taf'ala kadhā" (it is most fitting that you do such-and-such), and "ahra an taf'ala" (it is more fitting that you do it).

Al-rashad: guidance and correctness, and its tanwin (indefiniteness) is for glorification.

The meaning: whoever believes in Allah has aimed for the means of salvation and that by which reward is obtained, because rashad is the cause of that.

Al-qasit: the active participle of (qasata), of the pattern (daraba), qasţan, with a fatha on the qaf, and qusuṭan with a damma on it, meaning: he deviated. It is like injustice (zulm), intending by it a person's wronging of himself through associating partners with Allah. In al-Kashshaf:

Al-Hajjaj said to Sa'id ibn Jubayr when he wished to kill him: "What do you say about me?" He said: "Qasit 'adil" (a deviator, and just). The people said: "How well he has spoken!" — they thought he had described him as just (qist, with a kasra on the qaf) and equitable — whereupon al-Hajjaj said: "O fools! He called me a wrongdoer and a polytheist," and he recited to them His saying, exalted is He, ﴿As for those who deviate, they will be fuel for Hell﴾ and His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Yet those who disbelieve ascribe equals to their Lord﴾ [al-An'am: 1]. End of quotation.

He likened the dwelling of the disbelievers in Hell to the dwelling of firewood in the fire, in the manner of ridicule and belittlement; that is, because of their ignorance they are like firewood that does not understand, as in His saying, exalted is He, ﴿So fear the Fire whose fuel is men and stones﴾ [al-Baqarah: 24].

The insertion of the verb (kanu) is to affirm their destined arrival at the Fire, as though they had been that way from a time long past.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 72, verses 16–17:

﴿And that: if they had remained steadfast upon the way, We would have given them abundant water to drink﴾ ﴿that We might test them therein. And whoever turns away from the remembrance of his Lord, He will make him enter a severe punishment﴾

All ten reciters agreed on opening the hamza of ﴿أنْ لَوِ اسْتَقامُوا﴾ (an-law-istaqamu). The clause ﴿أنْ لَوِ اسْتَقامُوا﴾ is coordinated with the clause ﴿أنَّهُ اسْتَمَعَ نَفَرٌ مِنَ الجِنِّ﴾ (Al-Jinn: 1). The wāw (و) belongs to the reported speech, not to what is reported, so its content is a second matter of what was revealed to the Prophet (ﷺ), and Allah commanded him to say it to the people. The implied sense is: "It was revealed to me that if the deviators had remained steadfast and submitted, Allah would not have afflicted them by withholding the rain."

The (أنْ) here is a lightened form of the heavy (إنّ), and the hamza-opened (أنْ) was used because what follows it is an object (ma'mul) of the verb ʾūḥiya (it was revealed), so it is in the sense of a verbal noun (maṣdar). Its noun is omitted, and it is the pronoun of the matter (ḍamīr al-sha'n), and its predicate is ﴿لَوِ اسْتَقامُوا﴾ to the end of the clause. The composition of the speech is: "It was revealed to me that Allah's giving them water in the event of their steadfastness..."

The pronoun in istaqamū may refer to the deviators (al-qāsiṭūn) without considering the restriction that they are of the jinn, and this is the return of a pronoun to a word considered in isolation from its referent, like your saying: "I have a dirham and half of it," meaning half of another dirham.

[Page 238]

It is also possible that it refers to something not mentioned in the speech but known from the context, since the surah is directed to alerting to the obstinacy of the polytheists and their attacks on the Qur'an. So the pronoun of istaqamū refers to the polytheists, and this is common in the pronouns of the third person in the Qur'an, and likewise demonstratives, as we have noted and pointed out. It is not appropriate for it to refer to the deviators among the jinn, since the jinn have no connection with drinking water.

Steadfastness upon the way (al-istiqāmah ʿalā al-ṭarīqah) means the uprightness of walking along the road, which is walking with knowledge of the road without crookedness or being deceived by its side paths.

The ṭarīqah is the road, and perhaps it is specific to the wide, clear road, as was mentioned just before in His saying ﴿كُنّا طَرائِقَ قِدَدًا﴾ (Al-Jinn: 11).

Steadfastness upon the way is an image (tamthīl) of the state of one characterized by righteous conduct and true belief, in the form of a traveler walking a straight course on a path. For this reason the definite article in al-ṭarīqah is for the genus, not for a specific known thing.

His saying ﴿لَأسْقَيْناهم ماءً غَدَقًا﴾ (We would have given them abundant water) is a promise of a reward for steadfastness in the religion, a good reward in this world which would be a sign of Allah's pleasure, and a glad tidings of the reward of the Hereafter. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿مَن عَمِلَ صالِحًا مِن ذَكَرٍ أوْ أُنْثى وهو مُؤْمِنٌ فَلَنُحْيِيَنَّهُ حَياةً طَيِّبَةً ولَنَجْزِيَنَّهم أجْرَهم بِأحْسَنِ ما كانُوا يَعْمَلُونَ﴾ (An-Nahl: 97).

In this is a warning that He may soon withhold the rain from them, so they fall into drought and hunger. This is what befell them after the Prophet's (ﷺ) migration to Medina and his supplication against them for years like the years of Joseph, for he supplicated with that in Medina in the qunut, as in the hadith of the two Sahihs from Abu Hurayrah. We have explained this in Surah al-Dukhan. On the day this verse was revealed they were in comfort of life, with palm trees and gardens, so the arrangement of the giving of water being consequent upon steadfastness on the way, as required by the conditional with the particle (law), indicates that what is meant is: We would have continued to give them abundant water, and that they are not walking the path of steadfastness, so He may soon withhold from them the irrigation. In this is a warning that if they persist in the crookedness of the way, the water will be withheld from them. By this, the causal clause "that We might test them therein" in His saying ﴿لِنَفْتِنَهم فِيهِ﴾ harmonizes with the preceding clause, since it becomes a reason for what is implied by the continuation of giving water, for it is a reason for the watering existing at the time of the revelation of the verse, and not a reason for the watering supposed in the apodosis of (law), because the apodosis of (law) is negated, so it is not suitable to be given as a reason. Rather, they are tested by the blessing they are in, so Allah wished to awaken their hearts that the continuance of the blessing upon them is a trial for them, so let it not deceive them. The lam of causation in His saying ﴿لِنَفْتِنَهم فِيهِ﴾ is a stable adverbial phrase in the position of a circumstantial qualifier (ḥāl) of ﴿ماءً غَدَقًا﴾ (abundant water), which is the flowing water for them in the springs, from the sky, beneath their gardens and in their crops, so it is a concomitant circumstance.

With this explanation the perplexity in drawing out the meaning of the verse and its causal relation disappears.

Al-ghadaq: with a fatha on the ghayn (marked) and a fatha on the dal, it is abundant, plentiful water.

The clause ﴿لِنَفْتِنَهم فِيهِ﴾ is an insertion (idmāj), so it is a parenthetical clause between the clause ﴿وأنْ لَوِ اسْتَقامُوا عَلى الطَّرِيقَةِ﴾ etc., and the clause ﴿ومَن يُعْرِضْ عَنْ ذِكْرِ رَبِّهِ﴾ etc.

Then the allusive (kināyah) warning derived from His saying ﴿وأنْ لَوِ اسْتَقامُوا عَلى الطَّرِيقَةِ لَأسْقَيْناهُمْ﴾ etc. was reinforced by the explicit warning in His saying (﴿ومَن يُعْرِضْ عَنْ ذِكْرِ رَبِّهِ نَسْلُكْهُ عَذابًا صَعَدًا﴾), meaning: if they turn away, their state changes to punishment, and We make them enter the paths of punishment.

Al-salk: its essential meaning is causing to enter, and its verb is both intransitive and transitive; it is said: salakahu, fa-salaka. Al-A'sha said:

كَما سَلَكَ السِّكِّيَّ في البابِ فَيْتَقُ
That is: the carpenter drove the nail into the door.
It was mentioned at His saying ﴿كَذَلِكَ نَسْلُكُهُ في قُلُوبِ المُجْرِمِينَ﴾ (Al-Hijr: 12) in Surah al-Hijr.

The verb salk is used here in the sense of the severity of the action's occurrence, by way of metaphor (isti'ārah), and it is a rare metaphor. The meaning: We punish him with a punishment from which there is no escape.

Ṣa'adan (ʿadhāban ṣaʿadan) is in the accusative by removal of the preposition, which is the particle of place, and it is a figurative place-expression indicating that when the punishment descends upon him, it encompasses him as a container encompasses what is contained.

The departure from the pronoun to the noun in His saying ﴿عَنْ ذِكْرِ رَبِّهِ﴾ instead of saying "from Our remembrance" or "from My remembrance" is because the situation requires an allusion to the reason for constructing the predicate: one who turns away from his Lord who created him, brought him into being and governed him is worthy of being made to enter a punishment that is ṣa'ad.

Al-ṣa'ad: the hard, overpowering one. It seems to come from the verbal noun of ṣaʿida (like fariḥa), when one ascends and rises, i.e., he ascends over his object and overcomes it, as one says ʿalāhu, meaning he gained power over him, ﴿وأنْ لا تَعْلُوا عَلى اللَّهِ﴾ (Al-Dukhan: 19).

The majority recited (nasluk-hu) with the nūn of majesty, so there is an iltifāt (shift of person) in it. ʿĀṣim, Ḥamzah, al-Kisā'ī, Yaʿqūb and Khalaf recited (yaslukuhu) with the yāʾ of the third person absent, so the hidden pronoun returns to his Lord.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 72, verses 16–17:

﴿And that: if they had remained steadfast upon the way, We would have given them abundant water to drink﴾ ﴿that We might test them therein. And whoever turns away from the remembrance of his Lord, He will make him enter a severe punishment﴾

All ten reciters agreed on opening the hamza of ﴿أنْ لَوِ اسْتَقامُوا﴾ (an-law-istaqamu). The clause ﴿أنْ لَوِ اسْتَقامُوا﴾ is coordinated with the clause ﴿أنَّهُ اسْتَمَعَ نَفَرٌ مِنَ الجِنِّ﴾ (Al-Jinn: 1). The wāw (و) belongs to the reported speech, not to what is reported, so its content is a second matter of what was revealed to the Prophet (ﷺ), and Allah commanded him to say it to the people. The implied sense is: "It was revealed to me that if the deviators had remained steadfast and submitted, Allah would not have afflicted them by withholding the rain."

The (أنْ) here is a lightened form of the heavy (إنّ), and the hamza-opened (أنْ) was used because what follows it is an object (ma'mul) of the verb ʾūḥiya (it was revealed), so it is in the sense of a verbal noun (maṣdar). Its noun is omitted, and it is the pronoun of the matter (ḍamīr al-sha'n), and its predicate is ﴿لَوِ اسْتَقامُوا﴾ to the end of the clause. The composition of the speech is: "It was revealed to me that Allah's giving them water in the event of their steadfastness..."

The pronoun in istaqamū may refer to the deviators (al-qāsiṭūn) without considering the restriction that they are of the jinn, and this is the return of a pronoun to a word considered in isolation from its referent, like your saying: "I have a dirham and half of it," meaning half of another dirham.

[Page 238]

It is also possible that it refers to something not mentioned in the speech but known from the context, since the surah is directed to alerting to the obstinacy of the polytheists and their attacks on the Qur'an. So the pronoun of istaqamū refers to the polytheists, and this is common in the pronouns of the third person in the Qur'an, and likewise demonstratives, as we have noted and pointed out. It is not appropriate for it to refer to the deviators among the jinn, since the jinn have no connection with drinking water.

Steadfastness upon the way (al-istiqāmah ʿalā al-ṭarīqah) means the uprightness of walking along the road, which is walking with knowledge of the road without crookedness or being deceived by its side paths.

The ṭarīqah is the road, and perhaps it is specific to the wide, clear road, as was mentioned just before in His saying ﴿كُنّا طَرائِقَ قِدَدًا﴾ (Al-Jinn: 11).

Steadfastness upon the way is an image (tamthīl) of the state of one characterized by righteous conduct and true belief, in the form of a traveler walking a straight course on a path. For this reason the definite article in al-ṭarīqah is for the genus, not for a specific known thing.

His saying ﴿لَأسْقَيْناهم ماءً غَدَقًا﴾ (We would have given them abundant water) is a promise of a reward for steadfastness in the religion, a good reward in this world which would be a sign of Allah's pleasure, and a glad tidings of the reward of the Hereafter. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿مَن عَمِلَ صالِحًا مِن ذَكَرٍ أوْ أُنْثى وهو مُؤْمِنٌ فَلَنُحْيِيَنَّهُ حَياةً طَيِّبَةً ولَنَجْزِيَنَّهم أجْرَهم بِأحْسَنِ ما كانُوا يَعْمَلُونَ﴾ (An-Nahl: 97).

In this is a warning that He may soon withhold the rain from them, so they fall into drought and hunger. This is what befell them after the Prophet's (ﷺ) migration to Medina and his supplication against them for years like the years of Joseph, for he supplicated with that in Medina in the qunut, as in the hadith of the two Sahihs from Abu Hurayrah. We have explained this in Surah al-Dukhan. On the day this verse was revealed they were in comfort of life, with palm trees and gardens, so the arrangement of the giving of water being consequent upon steadfastness on the way, as required by the conditional with the particle (law), indicates that what is meant is: We would have continued to give them abundant water, and that they are not walking the path of steadfastness, so He may soon withhold from them the irrigation. In this is a warning that if they persist in the crookedness of the way, the water will be withheld from them. By this, the causal clause "that We might test them therein" in His saying ﴿لِنَفْتِنَهم فِيهِ﴾ harmonizes with the preceding clause, since it becomes a reason for what is implied by the continuation of giving water, for it is a reason for the watering existing at the time of the revelation of the verse, and not a reason for the watering supposed in the apodosis of (law), because the apodosis of (law) is negated, so it is not suitable to be given as a reason. Rather, they are tested by the blessing they are in, so Allah wished to awaken their hearts that the continuance of the blessing upon them is a trial for them, so let it not deceive them. The lam of causation in His saying ﴿لِنَفْتِنَهم فِيهِ﴾ is a stable adverbial phrase in the position of a circumstantial qualifier (ḥāl) of ﴿ماءً غَدَقًا﴾ (abundant water), which is the flowing water for them in the springs, from the sky, beneath their gardens and in their crops, so it is a concomitant circumstance.

With this explanation the perplexity in drawing out the meaning of the verse and its causal relation disappears.

Al-ghadaq: with a fatha on the ghayn (marked) and a fatha on the dal, it is abundant, plentiful water.

The clause ﴿لِنَفْتِنَهم فِيهِ﴾ is an insertion (idmāj), so it is a parenthetical clause between the clause ﴿وأنْ لَوِ اسْتَقامُوا عَلى الطَّرِيقَةِ﴾ etc., and the clause ﴿ومَن يُعْرِضْ عَنْ ذِكْرِ رَبِّهِ﴾ etc.

Then the allusive (kināyah) warning derived from His saying ﴿وأنْ لَوِ اسْتَقامُوا عَلى الطَّرِيقَةِ لَأسْقَيْناهُمْ﴾ etc. was reinforced by the explicit warning in His saying (﴿ومَن يُعْرِضْ عَنْ ذِكْرِ رَبِّهِ نَسْلُكْهُ عَذابًا صَعَدًا﴾), meaning: if they turn away, their state changes to punishment, and We make them enter the paths of punishment.

Al-salk: its essential meaning is causing to enter, and its verb is both intransitive and transitive; it is said: salakahu, fa-salaka. Al-A'sha said:

كَما سَلَكَ السِّكِّيَّ في البابِ فَيْتَقُ
That is: the carpenter drove the nail into the door.
It was mentioned at His saying ﴿كَذَلِكَ نَسْلُكُهُ في قُلُوبِ المُجْرِمِينَ﴾ (Al-Hijr: 12) in Surah al-Hijr.

The verb salk is used here in the sense of the severity of the action's occurrence, by way of metaphor (isti'ārah), and it is a rare metaphor. The meaning: We punish him with a punishment from which there is no escape.

Ṣa'adan (ʿadhāban ṣaʿadan) is in the accusative by removal of the preposition, which is the particle of place, and it is a figurative place-expression indicating that when the punishment descends upon him, it encompasses him as a container encompasses what is contained.

The departure from the pronoun to the noun in His saying ﴿عَنْ ذِكْرِ رَبِّهِ﴾ instead of saying "from Our remembrance" or "from My remembrance" is because the situation requires an allusion to the reason for constructing the predicate: one who turns away from his Lord who created him, brought him into being and governed him is worthy of being made to enter a punishment that is ṣa'ad.

Al-ṣa'ad: the hard, overpowering one. It seems to come from the verbal noun of ṣaʿida (like fariḥa), when one ascends and rises, i.e., he ascends over his object and overcomes it, as one says ʿalāhu, meaning he gained power over him, ﴿وأنْ لا تَعْلُوا عَلى اللَّهِ﴾ (Al-Dukhan: 19).

The majority recited (nasluk-hu) with the nūn of majesty, so there is an iltifāt (shift of person) in it. ʿĀṣim, Ḥamzah, al-Kisā'ī, Yaʿqūb and Khalaf recited (yaslukuhu) with the yāʾ of the third person absent, so the hidden pronoun returns to his Lord.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 72, verse 18:

﴿And the mosques are for Allah, so do not invoke anyone along with Allah.﴾ The ten readers (al-qurra' al-'ashara) agreed on opening the hamzah in ﴿wa-anna al-masajida lillah﴾. It is therefore coordinated (ma'tufah) with the object of the verb in ﴿It has been revealed to me that a group of the jinn listened﴾ [al-Jinn: 1], and its content is among the things revealed to the Prophet ﷺ and commanded to be conveyed. The meaning is: Say, "It has been revealed to me that the mosques are for Allah." Thus the verbal noun formed with "anna" and its subject and predicate is the deputy subject (na'ib fa'il) of "uhiya" (it was revealed).

The estimate is: "It has been revealed to me that the mosques are exclusively for Allah," that is, for His worship, since they were built only so that Allah would be worshipped in them, and they are the markers of monotheism (tawhid).

On this reading Sibawayh (Sibawayh) interpreted the verse, and Abu 'Ali (Abu 'Ali al-Farisi) followed him in al-Hujjah.

Al-Khalil (al-Khalil ibn Ahmad) held that the sentence is elided of a preposition (lam al-jarr) before "anna," so the prepositional phrase is placed before its governing element for emphasis. The estimate is: "And because the mosques are for Allah, do not invoke anyone along with Allah."

The lam in His saying "lillah" is the lam of entitlement (al-istihqaq), meaning that Allah alone deserves them, not the idols and images. Whoever places idols in the mosques of Allah has transgressed against Allah.

The intended mosque here is the Sacred Mosque (al-Masjid al-Haram), because the polytheists had placed idols in it and set the idol Hubal on the roof of the Ka'bah. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And who is more unjust than one who prevents the mosques of Allah from having His name mentioned therein and strives toward their ruin?﴾ [al-Baqarah: 114], meaning by that the polytheists of Quraysh.

This is a rebuke of the polytheists for their transgression upon the right of Allah and their interference in what was not theirs to change. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And they bar [others] from al-Masjid al-Haram, though they were not its guardians﴾ [al-Anfal: 34]. He used the plural form "mosques" (masajid) in this verse and in the verse ﴿And who is more unjust than one who prevents the mosques of Allah﴾ [al-Baqarah: 114] so that it would include those who do as they did and resemble them among those who alter mosques, or to magnify the Sacred Mosque. Likewise He used the plural "My messengers" (rusuli) in His saying ﴿So they denied My messengers, and how was My reproach?﴾ [Saba': 45], on the assumption that the pronoun in "kadhdhabu" refers back to ﴿those who disbelieved﴾ [Saba': 43] in His saying ﴿And those who disbelieved said of the truth when it came to them, "This is not but obvious magic"﴾ [Saba': 43], meaning: they denied My messenger.

From this is His saying ﴿And the people of Noah when they denied the messengers, We drowned them﴾ [al-Furqan: 37], meaning Noah, who was the first messenger, so he is the one intended by the plural.

Upon the exclusivity of the mosques belonging to Allah is based the prohibition against invoking anyone along with Allah. This is a binding upon them to affirm monotheism by way of "qawl bil-muwjab" (argument from their own premise), since they used to claim that they were the people of the House of Allah, so their worship of other than Allah contradicts that claim.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 72, verses 19–20:

﴿And when the servant of Allah stood up calling upon Him, they almost became around him a crowd.﴾ ﴿He said, "I only call upon my Lord, and I associate with Him no one."﴾

Nafi' alone, and Abu Bakr from 'Asim, read the hamza with a kasra (inna). The rest of the ten readers, in their well-known transmissions, read it with a fatha (anna).

The outcome of both readings is the same, in that this is outside what was said by the jinn, and in that it is part of what Allah revealed.

The kasra of the hamza is based on the conjunction of this sentence with the sentence ﴿It has been revealed to me﴾ [al-Jinn: 1], and the implied meaning is: "And say, indeed it is that when the servant of Allah stood up calling upon Him...". This is because the hamza of (inna) is pronounced with a kasra when it occurs in a statement introduced by a verb of saying. It is not fitting to take it as a quotation of the speech of the jinn, because that has ended and receded, and the discourse has moved on to other purposes beginning with His words ﴿And that the mosques are for Allah﴾ [al-Jinn: 18].

As for the fatha, it is based on considering it conjoined to the sentence ﴿that a company of the jinn listened﴾ [al-Jinn: 1], meaning: "And it was revealed to me that it is that when the servant of Allah stood up...", i.e., Allah revealed to me that the polytheists were close to becoming a crowd against the servant of Allah when he stood up calling upon his Lord.

The pronoun in (innahu) is the pronoun of the matter (dhamir al-sha'n), and the clause ﴿when the servant of Allah stood up﴾ up to its end is its predicate.

The pronoun in ﴿they almost became﴾ refers to the polytheists, indicated by the context in the third person and second person, beginning from His words ﴿And that if they had remained upon the way﴾ [al-Jinn: 16] up to His words ﴿so do not call upon anyone along with Allah﴾ [al-Jinn: 18].

"The servant of Allah" is Muhammad (ﷺ). The apparent noun was placed in the position of the pronoun, since the expected form would be: "And it is that when you stood calling upon Allah, they almost became against you," or "when I stood calling upon Allah, they almost became against me." Rather, he turned to the apparent noun in order to honour the Prophet (ﷺ) by the description "servant of Allah," because of the distinction contained in this idafa together with the description "servant" ('abd), as was mentioned more than once before, in his words ﴿Glory be to the One who took His servant by night﴾ [al-Isra': 1].

"Libadan" (لِبَدًا), with a kasra on the lam and a fatha on the ba' (with a shadda-less letter), is a collective noun (ism jam'): its singular is "libdah," which is what is matted together, one part upon another; from it comes "libdat al-asad" (the lion's mane), for the hair piled up on its neck.

The speech is in the mode of simile, meaning: the polytheists almost became like matted layers, pressing together and drawing close to him, listening to his recitation and his call to the Oneness of Allah. This is a gathering of rage, anger and intent to harm, as one says: "they banded together against him" (ta'allabu 'alayhi).

The meaning of "stood" (qama) is: he strove in calling to Allah, as in His saying, exalted is He, ﴿when they stood up and said: Our Lord is the Lord of the heavens and the earth﴾ [al-Kahf: 14] in Surat al-Kahf, and al-Nabigha said:

"That the fortress and the tribe of Banu Asad stood up and said: Our protection is not to be disputed."

It has already been mentioned regarding His saying, exalted is He, ﴿and establish the prayer﴾ [al-Baqarah: 3] at the beginning of Surat al-Baqarah.

The meaning of the Prophet's (ﷺ) standing is his proclamation of the call and the emergence of his call. Juz' ibn Kulayb al-Faq'asi said:

"So do not desire them, O son of Kawz, for indeed he has nourished the people since the Prophet stood up, the girls [i.e., the young women]."

That is, he stood worshipping Allah alone, as is indicated by his explanation after it in His words ﴿He said, "I only call upon my Lord, and I associate with Him no one."﴾ So when they were not accustomed to calling upon anything other than the idols, they gathered against them for this great event, which is the calling of Muhammad (ﷺ) upon Allah, exalted is He.

The sentence ﴿Say, "I only call upon my Lord, and I associate with Him no one."﴾ is an explanation of the clause (yad'uhu).

The majority read (qala) in the past tense. Hamza, 'Asim and Abu Ja'far read (qul) without an alif, in the imperative form, so the sentence is a new resumptive statement. The implied meaning is: "It was revealed to me that it is that when the servant of Allah stood up... say: I only call upon my Lord," so it is part of what was revealed to him.

"Innama ad'u rabbi" (﴿إنَّما أدْعُو رَبِّي﴾) conveys restriction (qasr), i.e., I call upon no other than Him, meaning I worship none other than Him.

"And I associate with Him no one" (﴿ولا أُشْرِكُ بِهِ أحَدًا﴾) is joined to it as an emphasis on the implied meaning of the restriction. Its original form is that it should not be conjoined, so its conjunction is merely for the sake of sharing the sense, with care for its independence in the conveying.

Commentary of Ibn ʿAshur (*al-Taḥrīr wa al-Tanwīr*) on Surah 72, verses 21–23:

﴿Say: "Indeed, I do not possess for you any harm or any right guidance."﴾ ﴿Say: "Indeed, none will protect me from Allah, and I will not find any refuge other than Him."﴾ ﴿But only a notification from Allah and His messages.﴾

This is an initial resumptive sentence (*istiʾnāf ibtidāʾī*, a new sentence that begins a fresh topic). It is a shift from mentioning what was revealed to the Prophet ﷺ to addressing him with a new speech. After this surah related what Allah revealed to His Messenger ﷺ about matters hidden from him, concerning those who followed and those who turned away, it moved to instructing him in how to answer those who showed him obstinacy and hostility.

It is possible that "﴿Say: 'Indeed, I do not possess'﴾" and what follows is a repetition of the sentence ﴿Say: "I only call upon my Lord"﴾ [al-Jinn: 20], according to the reading of Ḥamzah, ʿĀṣim and Abū Jaʿfar.

"Ḍurr" (harm) refers to what they used as a pretext for hostility, namely their demand that he bring about the victory over them that he had threatened them with.

His saying ﴿and not right guidance﴾ is a completion (*tatmīm*, adding a phrase to complete the meaning).

In the speech there is *iḥtibāk* (a device in which one element is omitted because its counterpart is mentioned, and vice versa), since harm is opposed by benefit, and right guidance is opposed by misguidance. The implied meaning is: "I do not possess for you harm or benefit, nor misguidance or right guidance."

"Al-Rashad" (with two fatḥahs) is the verbal noun of *rashada*, while "al-Rushd" (with a ḍammah and then a sukūn) is the noun, meaning knowledge of what is correct. It has already been mentioned shortly before in His saying ﴿guides to right conduct﴾ [al-Jinn: 2].

[Page 245 marker omitted from the translation.]

The construction "lā amliku lakum" means: I have no power, for your sake, over harm or benefit. It was discussed earlier at His saying ﴿And I have no power for you against Allah in anything﴾ [al-Mumtahanah: 4] in Surat al-Mumtahanah, and also earlier in Surat al-Aʿrāf.

The two clauses ﴿Say: "Indeed, none will protect me"﴾ up to ﴿refuge﴾ are parenthetical (*iʿtirāḍ*, an interjected phrase) placed between the excepted element and the exception. It is an interjection that responds to what they were trying to get from him: that he should leave off what hurts them, and not mention the Qur'an's refutation of their belief or its disparagement of their idols. Allah says: ﴿And when Our clear verses are recited to them, those who do not expect to meet Us say, "Bring us a Qur'an other than this or change it." Say, "It is not for me to change it on my own accord. I only follow what is revealed to me. Indeed, I fear, if I disobey my Lord, the punishment of a great Day."﴾ [Yūnus: 15].

"Al-Multaḥad" is the noun of place of *iltiḥād*, and *iltiḥād* is an intensification of *laḥd*, which is deviating to a place other than the one one is in. Most often this term is used for seeking refuge, i.e., seeking protection in a place that will safeguard him. The meaning is: "I will not find a place that will protect me."

"Min dūnihi" (other than Him) is a circumstantial element (*ḥāl*) of "multaḥadan," meaning: a refuge existing apart from Allah, i.e., far from Allah and not entering His dominion. Since "multaḥad" is a place, when it is described as "other than Allah," the meaning becomes that it is a place outside the places that are within Allah's dominion, and that is impossible. For this reason the particle "lan," which indicates the perpetuity of the negation, is used to negate finding it.

The "min" in His saying "min dūnihi" is a superfluous preposition (*mazīdah jārrah*) introducing the adverb "dūna."

His saying ﴿But only a notification from Allah and His messages﴾ is a disjunctive exception (*istithnāʾ munqaṭiʿ*, an exception not of the same kind as what precedes it) from "ḍarran" (harm) and "rashadan" (right guidance). It is not a connected exception (*muttaṣil*), because the harm and the right guidance negated in His saying ﴿I do not possess for you harm or right guidance﴾ are the harm and right guidance that come upon the soul by compulsion.

It is possible that it is also an exception from "multaḥadan," with "multaḥadan" interpreted to mean "a means of deliverance" or "a place of safety."

This implies that they continued to think they would prevail and succeed, *until*, when they see what they are promised, they realize that their hopes have failed.

(*Ḥattā*) here is inceptive (*ibtidā'iyyah*), and whenever (*ḥattā*) enters a sentence that begins with (*idhā*), then (*ḥattā*) is for beginning and what follows it is an inceptive sentence. Al-Akhfash and Ibn Malik held that (*ḥattā*) in such a construction is a preposition (*jārrah*) and that (*idhā*) is in the position of a genitive (*jarr*), and this is not far-fetched.

Know that "*ḥattā*" never loses the meaning of end-point, however its grammatical function varies.

(*Idhā*) is a noun of time referring to the future, implicitly carrying the meaning of a conditional, and it is in the position of an accusative (*naṣb*) governed by the verb in its answer, which is (*fa-sa-ya'lamūn*).

According to the view of al-Akhfash and Ibn Malik, (*idhā*) is in the position of a genitive governed by (*ḥattā*). The linking of the answer clause (*sa-ya'lamūn*) with (*fa*) is evidence that (*idhā*) carries the meaning of a conditional, and the linking of the answer with the future particle (*sīn*) turns the past verb after (*idhā*) toward future time. The clause that (*idhā*) is attached to is given as a past verb in order to draw attention to the certainty of its occurrence.

The verb (*sa-ya'lamūn*) is suspended from acting upon its object because an interrogative (*istifhām*) follows it. This is a very common usage of suspension, because the interrogative, with the vagueness inherent in it, serves as a metaphor for strangeness, such that people ask about specifying a thing after searching for it.

**Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 72, verse 28:**

﴿And He encompasses what is with them, and has counted everything in number.﴾ The *waw* here is either the *waw* of circumstance (*waw al-hal*), or it is parenthetical (*i'tirradiyyah*). Its content serves as a concluding generalization (*tadhyil*) to the clause ﴿that He may know that they have conveyed the messages of their Lord﴾. That is, He encompasses everything that is with the Messengers of conveyance and other matters, and He encompasses everything else besides that. So His saying ﴿and He encompasses what is with them﴾ is a generalization following the specification of what came before it, namely His knowledge of their conveying what they were sent with. His saying ﴿and has counted everything in number﴾ is a more comprehensive generalization following the generalization *ma* ("what").

He expressed knowledge by "counting" (*al-ihsa'*) as a metaphor (*isti'arah*), likening knowledge of things to knowledge of numbers, because knowledge of numbers is firmer. His saying ﴿in number (ʿadadan)﴾ is a supporting element (*tarshih*) for the metaphor.

*Al-ʿadad* (with the two letters separated, *al-ʿadad*) is, as a noun, the name for a counted thing; with the two letters merged (*al-ʿadd*), it is the verbal noun of *ʿadda* ("to count"). The meaning here, then, is: and He has counted everything as a counted thing (*maʿdudan*), and it is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (*hal*). This is unlike His saying, exalted is He, ﴿and He has counted them with a counting (*ʿaddan*)﴾ [Maryam: 94]. The Arabs distinguished between the verbal noun (*masdar*) and the object (*maf'ul*), because the object is more deeply nominal than the verbal noun, so it is further removed from merging (*idgham*), since merging is originally for verbs.

Surah al-Muzzammil

This surah has no name other than "Surat al-Muzzammil". It is known by an annexation (*idafah*) to this expression occurring at its beginning. It is therefore permissible that by it is meant the quoting of the word itself, and it is permissible that by it is meant the Prophet (ﷺ) described by the state in which he was addressed in His saying, exalted is He, ﴿O you who are wrapped up﴾ [al-Muzzammil: 1].

Ibn 'Atiyyah said: It is Meccan according to the view of the majority, except His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Indeed, your Lord knows that you stand [in prayer] almost two-thirds of the night﴾ [al-Muzzammil: 20] up to the end of the surah; that part is Medinan. Al-Qurtubi reported something similar from al-Tha'labi.

In *al-Itqan* (al-Suyuti) it is said: The exception of His saying, ﴿Indeed, your Lord knows that you stand [in prayer] almost two-thirds of the night﴾ [al-Muzzammil: 20] to the end of the surah is refuted by what al-Hakim reported from 'Aisha: it was revealed a year after the beginning of the surah was revealed, at the time when the night prayer was made obligatory at the beginning of Islam, before the obligation of the five daily prayers. End of quotation.

[p. 253]

That is, all of that was in Mecca. So the whole surah is Meccan, and it is determined that His saying, ﴿Stand [in prayer] through the night﴾ [al-Muzzammil: 2] was commanded in Mecca.

The reports are consistent that His saying, ﴿Indeed, your Lord knows that you stand﴾ [al-Muzzammil: 20] to the end of the surah was revealed separately from the revelation of what precedes it, after an interval whose length is disputed. 'Aisha said: it was revealed a year after the beginning of the surah. Al-Tabari reported something similar from Ibn 'Abbas. The majority said: the beginning of the surah was revealed in Mecca, and ﴿Indeed, your Lord knows﴾ [al-Muzzammil: 20] to its end was revealed in Medina, that is, years after the revelation of its beginning.

The apparent and more correct view is that the revelation of ﴿Indeed, your Lord knows﴾ [al-Muzzammil: 20] to the end of the surah took place in Medina, because of His saying, exalted is He, ﴿and others fight in the cause of God﴾ [al-Muzzammil: 20], unless that is a foretelling of the unseen in the manner of a miracle.

Al-Tabari reported from Sa'id ibn Jubayr that he said: When God revealed to His Prophet (ﷺ) ﴿O you who are wrapped up﴾, the Prophet (ﷺ) remained in this state for ten years, standing in prayer through the night as God had commanded him, and a group of his companions used to stand with him. Then God revealed, after ten years, ﴿Indeed, your Lord knows that you stand﴾ [al-Muzzammil: 20] to ﴿and establish the prayer﴾ [al-Muzzammil: 20]. End of quotation. That is: the final verses were revealed in Medina, on the basis that the Prophet's (ﷺ) stay in Mecca was ten years. This is the view of a great, numerous group.

The reports from 'Aisha are inconsistent. Some of them imply that the whole surah is Meccan, and that its first part was revealed a year before its last part, before the prayer was made obligatory. This is what al-Hakim reported, as quoted by the author of *al-Itqan*. That implies the beginning of the surah was revealed in Mecca. Some reports say that she used to spread a mat (*hasir*) for the Messenger of God (ﷺ), and he prayed on it during the night. People heard of this and gathered, and he went out angry, fearing that the night prayer would be prescribed for them. Then ﴿O you who are wrapped up﴾ [al-Muzzammil: 1] and ﴿Stand [in prayer] through the night, except a little﴾ [al-Muzzammil: 2] were revealed. So it was prescribed for them as a binding duty, and they remained at it for eight months. Then God lifted it from them, and He revealed ﴿Indeed, your Lord knows that you stand [in prayer] almost two-thirds of the night﴾ [al-Muzzammil: 20] to ﴿and He has turned to you in forgiveness﴾ [al-Muzzammil: 20]. So He returned them to the obligation and removed the supererogatory (*nafilah*) from them. This is what al-Tabari reported through two chains to Abu Salamah ibn 'Abd al-Rahman, from 'Aisha. It implies that the whole surah is Medinan, because the Prophet (ﷺ) did not consummate his marriage with 'Aisha except in Medina, and because her saying "he went out angry" implies that he went out from his house that opened onto his mosque. This is supported by reports establishing the night prayer in his mosque.

[p. 254]

Perhaps the cause of this inconsistency is a confusion in the transmission between the obligation of the night prayer and the encouragement to it.

Al-Qurtubi attributed to the *Tafsir* of al-Tha'labi that he said: al-Nakha'i said, concerning His saying, exalted is He, ﴿O you who are wrapped up﴾ [al-Muzzammil: 1]: The Prophet (ﷺ) was wrapped in 'Aisha's *qatifah*, which is a *mirt* (a cloak), half of it over her while she slept and half over the Prophet (ﷺ) while he prayed. End of quotation. But the Prophet (ﷺ) consummated his marriage with 'Aisha only in Medina. So what we rely on is that the beginning of the surah was certainly revealed in Mecca, as we will explain at His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Indeed, We will confer upon you a heavy word﴾ [al-Muzzammil: 5]. And His saying, ﴿Indeed, your Lord knows that you stand﴾ [al-Muzzammil: 20] to the end of the surah was revealed in Medina, years after the revelation of the beginning of the surah. This is because it contains an abrogation (*naskh*) of the obligation of the night prayer. Furthermore, the claim that the night prayer was the first thing made obligatory, before the prayer, as reported from 'Aisha, is strange (*gharib*).

Al-Qurtubi reported from al-Mawardi that Ibn 'Abbas and Qatadah said: two verses, namely ﴿and be patient over what they say﴾ [al-Muzzammil: 10] to His saying ﴿and leave them alone for a little while﴾ [al-Muzzammil: 11], were revealed in Medina.

Regarding the counting of this surah in the order of the revelation of surahs, there is disagreement. The most correct view, which the sound reports agree upon, is that the first surah revealed was al-'Alaq. Disagreement exists about what was revealed after al-'Alaq. It was said: Surat (Nun, wal-Qalam). It was also said that after al-'Alaq al-Muddaththir was revealed, and this appears to be the more preferred view. Then it was said that al-Muzzammil was revealed after al-Qalam, making it the third. This is the view of Jabir ibn Zayd in enumerating the order of the revelation of surahs. On the view that al-Muddaththir is the second, it is possible that al-Qalam is third and al-Muzzammil fourth, and it is possible that al-Muzzammil is third and al-Qalam fourth. The majority hold that al-Muddaththir was revealed before al-Muzzammil, and this is the apparent meaning of the hadith of 'Urwah ibn al-Zubayr from 'Aisha on the beginning of revelation in the *Sahih* of al-Bukhari, which will come at His saying, exalted is He, ﴿O you who are wrapped up﴾ [al-Muzzammil: 1].

The more correct view is that the occasion of revelation of ﴿O you who are wrapped up﴾ [al-Muzzammil: 1] is what is in the hadith of Jabir ibn 'Abd Allah, which will come at His saying, exalted is He, ﴿O you who are wrapped up﴾ [al-Muzzammil: 1], the verse.

The number of its verses according to the counting of the people of Medina is eighteen verses. According to the counting of the people of Basra it is nineteen. According to the counting of all others it is twenty.

* * *

**Its purposes:**

Conveying God's gentle kindness toward His Messenger (ﷺ) by addressing him with a description of his state of being wrapped up.

It includes the command to the Prophet (ﷺ) to stand in prayer for most of the night; praise of a group of the believers who forced themselves to stand in prayer at night.

The strengthening of the Prophet (ﷺ) in bearing the burden of conveying the revelation.

The command to persist in establishing the prayer, paying the zakat, and giving charity.

His command to devote himself wholly to carrying out what God commanded him of conveying, and to rely upon Him alone.

His command to turn away from the denial of the polytheists.

God's guarantee to him of victory over them, and that their recompense lies in God's hand.

The threat to them of the punishment of the Hereafter.

Admonishing them with what befell the people of Pharaoh when they denied the Messenger of God sent to them.

Mention of the Day of Resurrection and a description of its terrors.

The abrogation of standing in prayer for most of the night, by being content with standing for part of it, in consideration of the recurring excuses.

The promise of a great reward for good deeds.

Hastening to repentance. Included within this is the etiquette of reciting the Qur'an and reflecting upon it.

That the deeds of the day are not replaced by standing in prayer at night.

In this surah there are obscure passages and subtle expressions, so you must reflect upon them.
